stories.title: Why Plane Tickets Might Cost More Soon
stories.headline_kid: Fighting far away in the Middle East is making jet fuel pricier, so some airlines are now charging passengers a little more.
summary: Cathay Pacific, a big airline based in Hong Kong that many Singaporeans fly with, announced it will raise its 'fuel surcharge' from 1 August. A fuel surcharge is like an extra top-up fee added to your ticket price to help cover the airline's cost of jet fuel.

The reason? Fighting in the Middle East has caused jet fuel prices to shoot up again. Just this past week, the price of oil even crossed US$100 a barrel before dropping back down to around US$97 — like a roller coaster that keeps climbing and dipping.

When oil becomes more expensive, airlines have to pay more to fill up their planes. Many airlines then 'pass on the cost' to passengers through surcharges, so tickets end up pricier for everyone, including families flying out of Changi Airport.

This matters because Singapore is a major travel hub. If more airlines follow Cathay Pacific's move, families planning holiday trips during the June or December school holidays might find airfares creeping up.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a flight for the holidays, tickets might cost a bit more than before.
lenses.family: Parents may need to budget extra for flights, especially for overseas trips.
lenses.friends: Classmates who are excited about upcoming holiday trips might hear their parents talking about pricier tickets.
lenses.nation: Singapore's Changi Airport is one of the world's busiest, so rising fuel costs can affect tourism and business travel here.
lenses.world: It shows how a conflict thousands of kilometres away can still affect the price of things we do every day, like flying to see family.

stories.title: America and China's Tax Tug-of-War
stories.headline_kid: The US just added new taxes on goods from China and 59 other countries, and China says it is not happy about it at all.
summary: The United States announced new 'tariffs' — extra taxes on goods brought in from other countries — ranging from 10 to 12.5 per cent. China was given the highest rate, and the US says this is because of concerns about forced labour in factories.

China's government responded quickly, saying it opposes all one-sided tariff moves and warning the US against starting a full-blown 'trade war', where countries keep taxing each other's goods back and forth.

Think of a tariff like a toll booth on a highway — every truck of goods that crosses the border has to pay extra before it can be sold. When that toll goes up, the price of the goods usually goes up too, and shoppers everywhere can feel it.

Singapore doesn't make the tariffs, but our country trades with almost everyone, including the US and China. If a trade war heats up between these two giant economies, it can affect shipping, business, and even prices of things Singaporeans buy, like electronics or toys.

lenses.me: Things you buy that are made in China or shipped through these countries, like gadgets or toys, could become slightly pricier.
lenses.family: Your family's household budget might feel a small pinch if import costs rise over time.
lenses.friends: This is the kind of news that might come up in Social Studies class when learning about trade and globalisation.
lenses.nation: Singapore is a trading nation — we buy and sell goods with countries all over the world, so a US-China trade war could slow down business here too.
lenses.world: A bigger trade war between two of the world's largest economies could slow down growth everywhere, not just in the US and China.

compo_words.meaning: to officially put a rule, tax or punishment into force

compo_phrases.example: The new tariffs could have a ripple effect on prices around the world.

stories.title: ASEAN Leaders Edge Closer to Sea Rules
stories.headline_kid: Southeast Asian countries say they are getting closer to finishing a rulebook for the crowded South China Sea, and they hope to finish it by the end of this year.
summary: Foreign ministers from ASEAN, the group of Southeast Asian countries that includes Singapore, met in Manila this week. One big topic was the 'Code of Conduct' — a set of rules meant to help countries share the busy South China Sea safely and peacefully.

This matters because the South China Sea is claimed, in part, by several countries, and tensions have been rising. In fact, just this week, the Philippines accused China's coast guard of firing water cannons at its ships near a disputed area called Scarborough Shoal.

ASEAN leaders now say they have made progress and are aiming to complete the Code of Conduct by the end of this year — a hopeful sign after years of slow talks. Think of it like neighbours finally agreeing on rules for sharing a common playground fairly.

Singapore has a big stake in this even though we don't have territorial claims there. Our port is one of the busiest in the world, and countless ships carrying goods for Singapore — from electronics to food — pass through these waters every single day.

lenses.me: Many of your toys, gadgets and even snacks likely travelled through the South China Sea on a cargo ship to reach Singapore.
lenses.family: Your family's everyday items depend on these shipping routes staying open and safe.
lenses.friends: This is a good topic to bring up if your class is learning about ASEAN or Singapore's role in the region.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies heavily on calm, predictable seas for trade, so peace in the South China Sea protects our economy.
lenses.world: A completed Code of Conduct could lower the risk of conflict between major powers in one of the world's busiest waterways.

stories.title: New Taxes on Medicine Could Raise Prices Everywhere
stories.headline_kid: The US wants to add new taxes on cheap medicines made in India, and experts say this could make medicine pricier for people all over the world, including us.
summary: India makes a huge amount of the world's 'generic' medicines — these are cheaper copies of brand-name drugs that work exactly the same way, kind of like how a school uniform from a regular shop does the same job as one from a fancy boutique.

US President Donald Trump has proposed new tariffs, or taxes, on these Indian generic medicines coming into America. India's medicine-making companies are now scrambling to figure out how this will affect their business.

Experts warn this could disrupt supply chains — the whole chain of factories, ships and shops that gets medicine from where it's made to where it's needed. This might push up medicine prices in the US and force Indian factories to change how they operate.

Singapore imports many generic medicines too, often from India, to keep healthcare affordable. If the global supply chain gets squeezed by these new tariffs, it could eventually cause small ripple effects on medicine prices or availability here as well.

lenses.me: The fever medicine or cough syrup you take when you're unwell might be part of this same global supply chain.
lenses.family: Parents managing family healthcare costs might notice changes in medicine prices over time.
lenses.friends: Classmates who take regular medication, like for allergies or asthma, could be affected if supplies get disrupted.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies on imported medicines to keep healthcare affordable, so global supply chain problems matter to us too.
lenses.world: This shows how connected our world's healthcare system is — a decision made in one country can affect medicine cabinets everywhere.

compo_words.meaning: not having a brand name; a cheaper version that works the same way
compo_words.example: The doctor recommended the generic medicine because it was just as effective and much cheaper.

compo_words.meaning: to interrupt or cause problems for something that is normally running smoothly
compo_words.example: The new tariffs could disrupt the supply of medicines to hospitals.

compo_words.meaning: the whole process of making and moving goods from factory to customer
compo_words.example: A problem at one factory can affect the entire supply chain.

compo_phrases.meaning: a result that causes further results, one after another
compo_phrases.example: The tariff could have a knock-on effect on medicine prices around the world.

compo_phrases.meaning: to prevent prices or expenses from rising
compo_phrases.example: Hospitals try to use generic medicines to keep costs down for patients.

questions: Why do you think it's important for medicine to remain affordable for everyone, not just rich people?

What do you think governments should do to make sure important medicines don't become too expensive?

stories.title: From Silence to Spotlight: Her Musical Theatre Dream
stories.headline_kid: A young performer training in Singapore, who was born with hearing loss, proved that hard work and courage can turn even a 'wild dream' into reality.
summary: Sabrina Wong was born with moderate-to-severe hearing loss in both ears. Growing up, she felt shy and often retreated into what she called 'my own world', unsure how to connect with people around her.

Every five to seven days, she has to change the tiny batteries in her hearing aids — small devices that help her hear and follow conversations. Without them, everyday chats would be much harder to catch.

Through years of speech therapy, music lessons and theatre training, Sabrina slowly built up her confidence. What once felt like an impossible dream — performing on stage in front of an audience — became something she could actually do.

This August, Sabrina will graduate from LASALLE College of the Arts in Singapore with a degree in musical theatre. She has already performed on stage, showing that a challenge like hearing loss doesn't have to stop anyone from chasing their dreams.

lenses.me: Her story shows that even if something feels hard or impossible, small steps of practice can help you get there.
lenses.family: Families of children with hearing loss or other challenges can feel encouraged that support and patience really do help.
lenses.friends: Classmates who know someone with hearing difficulties can learn to be more patient and understanding.
lenses.nation: Singapore's arts schools, like LASALLE, show how our education system supports students with different needs to follow their passions.
lenses.world: Her journey is a reminder to people everywhere that determination can help overcome big obstacles.
